title: Immunometabolic regulation of macrophage function in cardio-hepatic-renal comorbidities: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: This review examines metabolic comorbidities affecting the heart, liver and kidney. The clinical prevalence of cardiohepatorenal metabolic comorbidities associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes is substantial. Chronic low-grade inflammation serves as the fundamental pathogenic mechanism. Abnormal macrophage activation is associated with metabolic disorders and damage to multiple organs. The conventional M1/M2 binary classification fails to adequately capture the heterogeneity of macrophages in vivo. Previous studies have primarily focused on the investigation of individual organs, leaving the cross-organ immune-metabolic linkage mechanism poorly understood. Furthermore, targeted interventions often lack precision. In this study, we systematically summarize the roles of macrophage polarization, phenotypic remodeling and metabolic activation in the injury of three metabolic organs. We also analyze their mediating functions in inter-organ immune-metabolic crosstalk and the associated pathological connections. Glycolipid toxicity impairs the glycolipid metabolism of macrophages via the NLRP3/SIRT pathway, resulting in a pro-inflammatory polarization advantage. Specific subsets of macrophages, including CCR2+,TREM2+,and CD206+CD68+,are involved in mediating myocardial remodeling, liver fibrosis, and renal interstitial injury, respectively.Medications such as SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists may provide multi-organ protection by modulating macrophage activity. The current research presents several limitations, including species differences between humans and mice, ambiguous temporal transformation rules of macrophages, and inadequate specificity of targeted preparations.Future efforts should leverage spatial multi-omics and gene editing technologies to analyze the global regulatory network and develop highly selective targeted strategies. This approach can offer theoretical support for the integrated and precise prevention and management of metabolic comorbidities.

title: The hypertension-NVU-cognition Axis: Mechanisms and interventions.
abstract: Midlife hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, but the specific molecular pathways through which it contributes to cognitive decline-pathways that are partially independent of, and interact with, amyloid-β pathology-are not fully elucidated. This review synthesizes and elaborates the "Hypertension-NVU-Cognition" axis, building on the established cerebrovascular biology, neurovascular unit, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and vascular cognitive impairment (VCID) literature, within which this axis is positioned as an integrative, complementary framework rather than a wholly novel or independent pathway. Sustained hypertension damages the neurovascular unit (NVU) through hemodynamic stress, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption (via tight junction and pericyte loss), and neuroinflammation (pro-inflammatory microglial activation and reactive astrogliosis). This NVU dysfunction directly impairs cognition via glutamate excitotoxicity, cholinergic axonal ischemia, and reduced Aβ clearance. Critically, midlife blood pressure trajectories are stronger predictors of late-life cognition than late-life levels. NVU injury frequently coexists with amyloid pathology, yet emerging evidence indicates it also contributes to cognitive decline in individuals with low amyloid burden, highlighting its complementary and potentially synergistic role alongside classical AD mechanisms. This axis highlights candidate molecular targets and biomarkers that merit further investigation for early intervention. Promising biomarkers include plasma sPDGFRβ (pericyte injury) and DCE-MRI Ktrans (BBB leakage). Promising future research directions include standardizing NVU biomarkers and conducting targeted trials that combine intensive blood pressure control with investigational NVU-protective agents (e.g., GLP-1 receptor agonists) in at-risk midlife individuals; these approaches are not yet clinically actionable and require validation in adequately powered randomized controlled trials. Understanding this axis is crucial for developing effective preventive therapies against vascular cognitive impairment.

title: Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Hyperuricemia, Serum Uric Acid and Gout: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Hyperuricemia and gout are common but underappreciated comorbidities in Type 2 diabetes (T2D), obesity and chronic kidney disease (CKD). We aimed to quantify the pooled effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 receptor agonists on serum uric acid (SUA), incident gout and hyperuricemia, and to determine whether these effects vary by drug class and are mediated by weight loss. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov through July 2026 for RCTs of ≥ 12 weeks' duration reporting SUA change, gout flares or hyperuricemia incidence. Random-effects meta-analysis, subgroup and sensitivity analyses and meta-regression were performed. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261468511). Eighteen RCTs (77 942 participants) met inclusion criteria. Incretin-based therapy significantly reduced SUA versus control (weighted mean difference [WMD] -0.44 mg/dL, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.35), reduced incident gout flares (hazard ratio [HR] 0.62, 95% CI 0.53-0.72), and reduced hyperuricemia incidence (odds ratio [OR] 0.61, 95% CI 0.53-0.70). Dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (tirzepatide) produced greater SUA lowering than mono GLP-1 RAs (-0.62 vs. -0.35 mg/dL, p = 0.001). Body-weight loss was a significant moderator of SUA reduction (β = -0.041 mg/dL per kg, p < 0.001), explaining 84.7% of between-trial heterogeneity, with a significant weight-independent intercept (-0.19 mg/dL, p < 0.001). The SUA reduction was robust in all sensitivity analyses, including restriction to placebo-controlled trials. GRADE certainty was high for SUA and moderate for gout flares (owing to small-study effects) and hyperuricemia incidence. Incretin-based therapies were associated with modest reductions in SUA and with a lower incidence of gout flares and hyperuricemia, an effect largely related to weight loss. The clinical relevance of these effects, and the mechanism of any weight-independent component, remains uncertain and warrant confirmation in dedicated trials.

title: Role of GLP1-receptor signaling and α-β communication in functional β-cell heterogeneity.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: While islet β-cells were first viewed as a singular functional entity, since the 1970s findings reveal that individual β-cells differ in their insulin secretion. More recently distinct functional subpopulations based on differential calcium dynamics have been demonstrated to drive islet function. Here, we investigate how paracrine signaling, specifically glucagon-like peptide receptor (GLP-1R) signaling shapes functional β-cell heterogeneity. To address this, we utilized confocal imaging of calcium responses of in-vitro islets from MIP-CreER-GCaMP6s mice, C57BL/6 mice, and β-cell-specific humanized GLP-1R Cre-inducible KO mice. Responses in isolated islets vs pancreatic slices both before and after GLP-1R antagonist (exendin-9) or agonist (exendin-4) treatment were compared. We employ consecutive glucose stimulations in the same islet, where first stimulation serves as a control for the second stimulation. Function of the β-cells was significantly enhanced in the 2 nd glucose stimulation, reflecting previously reported time-dependent glucose potentiation phenomenon. GLP-1R antagonism delayed response time, decreased peak amplitude, active time and oscillation frequency, and disrupted the temporal consistency of hub-cells and 1 st responder β-cells, relative to the 1 st stimulation. Opposite effects were observed with the GLP-1R agonist. The changes in Ca 2+ frequency were more pronounced in α-neighboring β-cells, suggesting local GLP-1R mediated α-β-cell communication. GLP-1R KO elicited deleterious effects, which, aside from the network connectivity, mirrored those of the ex-9. Together, these findings underscore the importance of GLP-1R-mediated α- and β-cell communication in heterogeneous β-cell function. Role of GLP-1R mediated α-β cell communication in functional β-cell heterogeneity was unclear. Time of response to glucose, 1 st phase amplitude, speed of signal propagation, active time, functional connectivity, and consistency of 1 st responder and hub cell subpopulations are enhanced by GLP-1R signaling. GLP-1R signaling creates local α-cell-associated functional neighborhoods of β-cells and maintains network organization.Islet-local GLP-1R communication in absence of exogenous GLP-1 is sufficient for significant control of β -cell function.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists as potential disease-modifying agents in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms, clinical trial evidence, and the neuroprotection horizon.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), originally developed as antidiabetic agents, have emerged as candidate disease-modifying therapies for Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), reflecting the widespread expression of GLP-1 receptors across neurons, glia, and the cerebral vasculature. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical trial, and biomarker evidence for GLP-1 RAs in PD and AD, based on a literature search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, with ClinicalTrials.gov searched separately for trial protocols and results, through May 2026. Preclinical data implicate GLP-1 receptor agonism in anti-neuroinflammatory signaling, mitochondrial preservation, autophagy and proteostasis enhancement, anti-apoptotic effects, synaptic plasticity, cerebrovascular protection, and glymphatic clearance. Clinical evidence in PD is mixed and agent- and formulation-dependent: the phase II Exenatide-PD trial reported a motor benefit that persisted after washout (∼3.5-point between-group difference in MDS-UPDRS Part III), and the phase II LIXIPARK trial (lixisenatide) reported a significant 3.08-point between-group difference (95% CI 0.86-5.30; p = 0.007) favoring lixisenatide, whereas the larger, longer phase III Exenatide-PD3 trial, using an extended-release weekly formulation, found no significant effect on the same endpoint (adjusted coefficient 0.92; 95% CI -1.56 to 3.39; p = 0.47); oral semaglutide is under investigation in the ongoing phase II MOST-ABLE trial. In AD, the phase IIb liraglutide (ELAD) trial did not achieve statistical benefit on either its primary imaging endpoint (cerebral glucose metabolic rate; p = 0.14) or on most secondary cognitive measures, and the phase III semaglutide trials EVOKE and EVOKE+ did not meet their primary CDR-SB endpoint (estimated difference -0.08, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.20, p = 0.57 in EVOKE; 0.10, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.38, p = 0.46 in EVOKE+), despite biomarker signals including reductions in cerebrospinal fluid tau species and inflammatory markers. Comparative pharmacology reveals substantial heterogeneity in central nervous system penetration, receptor engagement, and systemic bioavailability across exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, and the imbalanced GLP-1/GIP co-agonist tirzepatide, complicating cross-agent extrapolation. Persistent challenges include separating direct neuroprotection from indirect metabolic and cardiovascular benefit, limited characterization of brain drug exposure, trial durations that may be short relative to the expected latency of a disease-modifying effect, and the absence of validated response biomarkers. We conclude that although the mechanistic and epidemiological rationale for GLP-1 RAs in neurodegeneration remains biologically plausible, current trial evidence does not yet support their use outside clinical trials, irrespective of comorbid diabetes status; future studies should prioritize earlier intervention, biomarker-guided patient selection, adequately powered subgroup analyses, and brain-penetrant formulations.

title: The impact of GLP-1 receptor agonists on chemotherapeutic efficacy: insights from GWAS and experiments.
abstract: Emerging evidence highlights the anti-tumor properties of Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). However, their synergistic potential with standard chemotherapy remains largely unexplored. Data from Genome-wide association study (GWAS) were used to select single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) strongly associated with lipid-lowering drug targets as instrumental variables. Causal effects were assessed primarily using the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method, supported by comprehensive sensitivity analyses to control for pleiotropy and heterogeneity. These Mendelian randomization (MR) findings were further validated through in vitro functional assays (cell viability, apoptosis, and Western blot) and an in vivo tumor-bearing mouse model. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activity showed a significantly positive causal relationship with dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR; β = 0.323, P = 6.02 × 10-17) and apoptosis regulator Bcl-2 (β = 0.259, P = 2.1 × 10-11) but a negative relationship with ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase large subunit (RRM1; β = -0.12, P = 2.32 × 10-3). Functional experiments validated these genetic findings. GLP-1RA significantly enhanced the antitumoral efficacy of gemcitabine both in vitro and in vivo by repressing RRM1. Conversely, GLP-1RA attenuated the anti-tumor effects of methotrexate and paclitaxel by upregulating DHFR and Bcl-2, respectively. Notably, GLP-1RA combination therapy achieved these modulatory effects without exacerbating chemotherapy-associated systemic toxicity. GLP1-RAs can influence the efficacy of chemotherapeutic drugs such as methotrexate, paclitaxel, and gemcitabine.

title: Metabolic and biochemical predictors of glycemic response after bariatric surgery: a scoping review.
abstract: Bariatric and metabolic surgery is one of the most effective treatments for severe obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), promoting metabolic changes beyond weight loss. However, the biochemical determinants of postoperative glycemic response remain incompletely understood. A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025 evaluating metabolic and biochemical variables associated with glycemic outcomes after bariatric surgery. Twenty-two studies were included, comprising eight randomized controlled trials and fourteen cohort studies. Bariatric surgery was consistently associated with reductions in HbA1c and significant rates of T2DM remission. Improvements in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), beta-cell function, and incretin response-particularly GLP-1-were associated with better outcomes. Reductions in inflammatory markers, including IL-6, IFN-γ, and TNF-α, were also reported. Glycemic improvement after bariatric surgery is associated with complex metabolic interactions involving insulin sensitivity, incretin modulation, and inflammatory changes. These findings support the role of bariatric and metabolic surgery as a metabolic and immunometabolic intervention, although the descriptive design of a scoping review precludes causal inference.

title: Molecularly guided pharmacotherapy for obesity: emerging targets, clinical efficacy, and personalized therapeutic approaches.
abstract: Obesity is a complex, chronic disease whose aetiology is complex and highly variable, and is linked to a network of neural, endocrine, adipose, genetic, epigenetic and metabolic pathways. This molecular complexity also drives significant differences in the clinical course of disease, drug sensitivity and weight regain, thus making standardized treatment, which is largely based on BMI and clinical empiricism, challenging. This narrative review explores the molecular mechanisms involved in obesity and the potential to apply the knowledge of molecular mechanisms to develop more personalized treatment strategies using advances in pharmacology. It focuses on hypothalamic appetite-satiety pathways, gut-brain hormonal communication, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction in adipose tissue, and known and novel drug targets. The review focuses on the evidence available on GLP-1 receptor agonism, GIP-GLP-1 co-agonism, multi-agonism with glucagon, signaling of amylin, melanocortin pathways, and novel central and peripheral targets. Studies have shown that some dual- and triple-receptor drugs are more effective at causing weight loss, and practitioners should consider tolerability, sustainability, cardiometabolic effects, and response when choosing drugs or drug combinations for patients. Inter-individual variability may be further explained by genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and tissue-specific factors, which may help identify mechanisms of resistance. In conclusion, Inter-individual variability may be attributed to genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and tissue-specific factors, and most suggested molecular or biomarker predictors have not yet proven sufficiently valid or useful for routine drug selection. Receptor-targeted drugs, including GLP-1 receptor agonists and GIP-GLP-1 co-agonists, are currently clinically actionable for patients with common obesity and available to specific patients with obesity, genotype-directed molecular therapeutic drugs are clinically actionable only for selected genetically defined types of obesity. However, the use of pharmacogenomic, biomarker, and multi-omics methods to guide the choice of anti-obesity drugs are still in their early stages of clinical investigation.

title: Common Genetic Variants Near SLC2A2 and Glycemic Response to Glimepiride in the GRADE Comparative Effectiveness Clinical Trial.
abstract: Optimizing second-line therapy for type 2 diabetes remains challenging because of interindividual variability in response. Current treatment selection does not consider personal genetic profiles. To address this gap, we conducted a pharmacogenomic genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a randomized comparative effectiveness trial to identify genetic predictors of glycemic response to insulin glargine, glimepiride, liraglutide, and sitagliptin when added to metformin. In the Glycemia Reduction Approaches in Type 2 Diabetes: A Comparative Effectiveness Study (GRADE), we performed a GWAS for the time to reach primary (glycated hemoglobin [HbA1c] ≥7%) and secondary (HbA1c >7.5%) metabolic failure. We conducted replication in independent cohorts, performed fine mapping of the top variants near SLC2A2, evaluated them for physiologic impact using oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) and response to acute glipizide challenge, and characterized glycemic response to glimepiride in an slc2a2-mutated zebrafish model. rs2129019 in SLC2A2 encoding GLUT2 was enriched in African/African American participants and conferred a 38% increased risk of metabolic failure per A allele on glimepiride (P = 1.55 × 10-8). Carriers had impaired β-cell function, evidenced by a lower C-peptide index during OGTT, and diminished glucose-lowering response to acute sulfonylurea challenge. Genetic manipulation in zebrafish confirmed that slc2a2 disruption attenuated the glucose-lowering effect of glimepiride. Genetic variation influences glycemic response to glucose-lowering medications, with SLC2A2 emerging as a genetic factor that modulates sulfonylurea response. These findings warrant further study to evaluate whether low-response allele carriers would benefit from alternative glucose-lowering therapies to advance precision diabetes care.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Across the Coronary Disease Continuum in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review of Ischemic Events, Revascularization, and Stent Healing.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is associated with accelerated coronary atherosclerosis, recurrent ischemic events, and impaired vascular healing after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI); however, the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists across these distinct coronary outcomes remain incompletely characterized. This systematic review synthesized randomized evidence on myocardial infarction (MI), acute coronary syndrome (ACS), coronary revascularization, post-PCI healing, and mechanistic markers of coronary disease. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were initially searched for eligible reports published from January 1, 2020, through December 31, 2025. All four database searches were updated on August 31, 2026, extending publication eligibility through that date; no additional eligible reports were identified. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. Seven eligible reports derived from seven parent randomized trials, involving 37,033 participants, were included. Two presented primary findings from independent randomized trials, three were prespecified analyses of parent randomized trials, and two were post hoc analyses. Owing to substantial clinical and outcome heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Albiglutide reduced first and recurrent MI, including type 1 and type 2 events, whereas higher-dose efpeglenatide yielded more favorable cardiovascular effect estimates than the lower dose. Across separate reports, semaglutide favorably modified epicardial adipose tissue, a surrogate imaging measure, and reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke in patients with diabetic kidney disease. Liraglutide was associated with lower risks of broader cardiovascular composites compared with the other glucose-lowering therapies combined, although individual MI and revascularization outcomes were not significantly reduced. Exenatide did not significantly reduce the composite of hospitalization for ACS or coronary revascularization, and the only PCI-specific trial demonstrated no significant improvement in early stent coverage, neointimal thickness, or in-stent obstruction. Of the seven included reports, one was judged to have a low risk of bias, whereas six raised some concerns, primarily because of post hoc analyses, open-label treatment, incomplete methodological reporting, or limited imaging follow-up. Across the included reports, findings were more favorable for MI and broader cardiovascular events than for coronary revascularization or post-stent healing. However, the small number of heterogeneous reports, reliance on several secondary or post hoc analyses, and absence of quantitative meta-analysis limit firm conclusions and do not establish a definitive class-wide coronary effect. Potential differences by agent, dose, and patient phenotype require further investigation, while treatment-initiation timing remains largely untested.

title: Gut microbiota and treatment response heterogeneity across pharmacological therapies for MASH.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a progressive liver disease with increasing global prevalence. However, substantial inter-individual variability in therapeutic response remains a major challenge for effective disease management. Although the gut microbiota is well recognized as a key contributor to MASH pathogenesis, its role in shaping pharmacological treatment response remains insufficiently understood and underexplored in clinical contexts. In this Review, we summarize evidence suggesting that gut microbiota-associated metabolites, including bile acids, short-chain fatty acids, sphingolipids, and other microbial products, may contribute to variability in therapeutic response across major pharmacological classes for MASH, including FXR agonists, PPAR agonists, FGF19/FGF21 analogues, thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists, and incretin-based therapies. However, for most therapeutic classes, direct clinical evidence linking microbiota features to inter-individual treatment response remains limited, and much of the mechanistic evidence is derived from preclinical studies. We integrate current evidence into a response-oriented conceptual framework linking microbiome composition and metabolic activity to biological processes relevant to drug efficacy. This framework identifies priorities for the prospective validation of microbiome-derived biomarkers and microbiome-informed patient stratification in MASH.

title: Diabesity: an old term, a modern challenge - multi-omics and precision anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in type 2 diabetes.
journal: Journal of pharmacy & pharmaceutical sciences : a publication of the Canadian Society for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Societe canadienne des sciences pharmaceutiques
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity are closely interconnected but heterogeneous conditions in which treatment response, safety, body weight, glycemic control, and long-term clinical outcomes vary substantially between individuals. This narrative review evaluates emerging anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with coexisting T2DM and obesity and examines the translational role of multi-omics in future precision treatment selection. Distinct from reviews focused primarily on obesity pharmacotherapy or omics-based disease stratification, the present review emphasizes the interface between contemporary drug mechanisms, T2DM-associated metabolic heterogeneity, candidate molecular signatures, and the level of evidence required for clinically actionable prescribing. We summarize evidence for approved and investigational oral incretin therapies, dual and triple receptor agonists, amylin-based strategies, established antidiabetic drugs, and adjunctive approaches targeting body composition. Throughout the review, we distinguish established clinical evidence from mechanistic rationale, candidate biomarkers, exploratory associations, and hypothetical future precision applications. We also separate metabolic efficacy endpoints, such as body weight and HbA1c, from intermediate cardiometabolic risk markers and from cardiovascular or kidney outcomes demonstrated in dedicated outcome trials. At present, no genomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, proteomic, microbiome, or integrated multi-omics signature has been clinically validated to select a specific anti-obesity medication for patients with T2DM and obesity. Major unresolved issues include the need for prospective biomarker validation, direct comparative trials, standardized assays, externally validated and calibrated prediction models, preservation of skeletal muscle health and physical function, long-term safety, treatment durability, affordability, and equitable implementation. Multi-omics should therefore be viewed as an investigational framework for generating and testing precision-treatment hypotheses rather than as a basis for routine prescribing.

title: Digital Augmentation of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 for Obesity Management: Retrospective Study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are highly effective for weight management; however, long-term outcomes depend on sustained behavioral engagement. Digital health tools may enhance these behavioral components, but evidence regarding their real-world benefit alongside pharmacotherapy remains limited. This study aims to evaluate whether augmenting a direct-to-consumer GLP-1 RA program with a behavioral support smartphone app improves weight-loss outcomes compared with medication alone, and to identify which app features are associated with weight loss over time. A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using data from 6113 adults (older than 18 years) in Australia who self-enrolled into the Mosh direct-to-consumer weight-loss program between July 1, 2024, and August 13, 2025, with their weight data recorded at baseline and at least 1 other timepoint. Participants received semaglutide or tirzepatide, with optional access to a smartphone app and clinician support. Logistic regression models examined achievement of ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight-loss thresholds at 60, 120, and 180 days. Linear mixed-effects models interacting with app feature use, with linear and quadratic time terms, assessed the association of different features with percentage weight loss trajectories over time. Both models adjusted for medication type, gender, ethnicity, age, and baseline BMI. Participants using the program plus medication had higher odds of achieving clinically significant weight loss than those using medication only. Adjusted odds ratio point estimates for day 60, 120, and 180 (±10) days indicated they were 1.38 (95% CI 1.09-1.75) times to 2.22 (95% CI 1.40-3.45) times more likely to achieve ≥5% weight loss across timepoints, 1.67 (95% CI 1.33-2.10) times to 1.97 (95% CI 1.35-2.90) times more likely to achieve ≥10% weight loss by day 120 and 180, and 1.99 (95% CI 1.26-3.29) times more likely to achieve ≥15% weight loss by 180 days. Mixed-effects modeling demonstrated that progress logging was associated with more rapid weight loss over time (β=.26 percentage-point additional weight lost per 30 days, SE 0.06; t4336=4.46; 95% CI 0.14-0.38; P<.001). No other app features were consistently associated with changes in weight-loss trajectories. Augmenting GLP-1 RA treatment with a behavioral smartphone app was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving clinically significant weight loss, although differences in overall weight-loss trajectories were modest. Progress logging emerged as the primary behavioral predictor of improved outcomes. While not causal effects, these findings are consistent with the positive value of integrating digital tools with pharmacotherapy for weight loss.

title: Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Death: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Cardioprotective Efficacy of Semaglutide.
abstract: Cardiovascular death (CVD) remains a leading cause of global mortality. Although semaglutide reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), the consistency and exact magnitude of its standalone effect on CVD across various patient phenotypes require comprehensive evaluation. This meta-analysis systematically evaluated the clinical efficacy of semaglutide on CVD risk across randomized controlled trials (RCTs). PubMed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to July 2026 to identify RCTs comparing semaglutide with placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), overweight or obesity, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or chronic kidney disease, reporting CVD as a primary, secondary or exploratory outcome. Pooled hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a random-effects restricted maximum likelihood (REML) model. Publication bias and study robustness were assessed via Egger's test, Begg's test, and trim-and-fill analysis. Seven high-quality RCTs comprising 38412 patients were included. Semaglutide significantly reduced the risk of CVD by 17% compared with placebo (pooled HR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72-0.95; P = 0.01). Inter-study heterogeneity was low-to-moderate (I 2= 27.44%, P = 0.18). Subgroup analyses confirmed uniform benefits across different clinical phenotypes (T2DM; overweight or obesity without diabetes; and obesity-related HFpEF, with or without T2DM; P = 0.63) and administration routes (oral versus subcutaneous; P = 0.74). Meta-regression identified trial duration as a key moderator (R 2 = 85.27%, P = 0.089), whereas sex, age, BMI, HbA1c and concomitant SGLT2i therapy did not modify the treatment effect. Publication bias tests were non-significant, and trim-and-fill simulations confirmed the stability of the primary pooled estimate. Semaglutide delivers a robust and consistent 17% reduction in CVD across diverse cardiometabolic populations, including patients with T2DM, overweight or obesity without diabetes, and obesity-related HFpEF. These findings strongly support its role as a foundational cardioprotective intervention, independent of baseline glycemic status or the administration route.

title: Efficacy and safety of semaglutide versus placebo in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes: updated meta-analysis of randomized trials.
journal: Journal of diabetes and metabolic disorders
abstract: Obesity poses significant challenges for those seeking long-term weight loss through diet and exercise alone. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for chronic weight management in eligible adults. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of semaglutide for treating obesity in adults without diabetes. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261338170). PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through February 28, 2026. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing semaglutide with placebo in adults without diabetes with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 or ≥ 27 kg/m2 and at least one obesity-related comorbidity. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 Tool, GRADE methodology, RevMan v5.4, and CMA v3 were used for risk-of-bias assessment, certainty-of-evidence assessment, data analyses, and meta-regression analyses respectively. We included 10 RCTs with a total of 7,131 participants. Risk-of-bias was judged at the level of each outcome: all included trials were at low risk-of-bias for the efficacy outcomes and the prespecified safety outcomes, while cardiovascular and psychiatric disorders raised some concerns. Compared to placebo, semaglutide produced significantly greater reductions in percentage change in body weight (WMD -12.29%, 95% CI -13.38 to -11.20, I2 88%, 95% PI -16.06 to -8.52; 10 studies, n = 6975), absolute change in body weight from baseline (WMD -12.67 kg, 95% CI -13.53 to -11.81, I2 77%, 95% PI -15.36 to -9.98; 10 studies, n = 6975), BMI (WMD -4.55 kg/m2, 95% CI -5.08 to -4.03, I2 86%, 95% PI -6.33 to -2.78; 8 studies, n = 6573), and waist circumference (WMD -9.42 cm, 95% CI -10.27 to -8.56, I2 79%, 95% PI -12.12 to -6.71; 10 studies, n = 6970). Participants assigned to semaglutide also had a higher probability of reaching a ≥ 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% loss of body weight (9 studies, n = 6103). However, substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed for efficacy outcomes, indicating that the magnitude of benefit varied across trials. With semaglutide, individuals experienced a greater number of total adverse events (aggregate proportions 90.0% vs. 85.0%; RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.10, I2 72%; 9 studies, n = 6922) and discontinuation due to adverse events (aggregate proportions 6.0% vs. 3.0%; RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.41 to 2.45, I2 0%; 10 studies, n = 7129) than did individuals taking the placebo; while for serious adverse events (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.51, I2 40%; 10 studies, n = 7129) the estimate was imprecise, did not establish a clear difference and the interval remains compatible with a potentially important increase in risk. These pooled figures represent average effects and may not apply equally across different semaglutide doses, formulations, treatment duration, or patient populations. Certainty-of-evidence was low for the primary outcome of percentage change in body weight and for absolute change in body weight and change in BMI, and very low for change in waist circumference. Semaglutide was associated with clinically meaningful weight loss during trial treatment periods in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes; however, low-certainty evidence and substantial between-study heterogeneity warrant cautious interpretation of the magnitude of benefit. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40200-026-02108-x.

title: Severe Infection Outcomes With SGLT2 Versus DPP-4 Inhibitors in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Active-Comparator Meta-Analysis of Real-World Cohorts.
abstract: To update and methodologically refine the synthesis of real-world evidence on severe infection outcomes with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) versus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i), emphasising limits of causal interpretation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 29 June 2026. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to DPP-4i active-comparator estimates. Incident pneumonia and sepsis were prespecified co-primary outcomes. Hazard ratios and incidence rate ratios were pooled as related but non-identical estimands using restricted maximum likelihood with modified Hartung-Knapp inference, with leave-one-out, prediction-interval and effect-measure-stratified analyses. ROBINS-I and GRADE were applied. Eighteen cohorts were included; the 11 contributing quantitatively were all at moderate risk of bias. For incident pneumonia (five studies), the pooled ratio was 0.65 (95% CI: 0.55-0.75; prediction interval 0.45-0.93; I2 = 89.8%; very low certainty); omitting one multinational cohort whose follow-up began 2 years after drug initiation yielded 0.61 (0.56-0.67; I2 = 0%). For incident sepsis (five studies), the prediction interval crossed the null (0.38-1.13); the exploratory pooled ratio was 0.65 (0.53-0.80; I2 = 90.6%, and 88.1%-92.4% after every omission; very low certainty). Hazard-ratio-only point estimates were similar, although the sepsis estimate was imprecise (95% CI including 1.0). Two cohorts reported identical, unpooled estimates for infection-related hospitalisation (0.74 each; low certainty). Comparisons with GLP-1 receptor agonists did not show a consistent lower-risk pattern across four cohorts, two in selected populations, and randomised-trial syntheses have not shown a consistent class-wide preventive effect. The available evidence did not suggest an increased average risk of severe infection with SGLT2i compared with DPP-4i. Given low to very low certainty and substantial heterogeneity, the lower pooled estimates should not be interpreted as a preventive effect. PROSPERO: CRD420261390509.

title: A test of the Tripartite Influence Model in the context of GLP-1 medication consideration among women in the United Kingdom.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications are increasingly used for weight loss, yet little is known about the sociocultural and psychological factors underlying interest in their use. One framework for understanding such factors is the Tripartite Influence Model (TIM), which proposes that sociocultural appearance pressures contribute to body dissatisfaction and eating pathology via appearance-ideal internalisation and appearance comparison processes. The present study aimed to apply the TIM to examine sociocultural predictors of GLP-1 medication consideration among women. Participants were 329 UK women (Mage = 38.16 years, SD = 12.62) recruited via Prolific, who completed measures of appearance pressure from media, family, peers, and significant others, thin-ideal internalisation, upward appearance comparison, body dissatisfaction, and GLP-1 medication consideration. Structural equation modelling was used to test the TIM. The model demonstrated excellent fit and explained 35.6% of the variance in GLP-1 consideration. Media pressure showed significant indirect associations with GLP-1 consideration through thin-ideal internalisation and through a direct effect on body dissatisfaction, though not through upward appearance comparison. Family pressure was indirectly associated with consideration through body dissatisfaction, but not through internalisation or comparison. Peer pressure showed a significant total indirect association with consideration, although the specific pathway through thin-ideal internalisation was marginal. Significant-other pressure showed no significant indirect effect on consideration through either internalisation or comparison. These findings represent the first application of the TIM to the consideration of GLP-1 medication for weight loss and suggest that sociocultural appearance pressures may shape interest in these medications through recognised body image processes.

title: Glycemic control and weight loss benefits of fixed-ratio combinations of basal insulins and GLP1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract: To compare glycemic and weight effects of fixed-ratio combinations (FRCs) of basal insulin (BI) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). Randomized controlled trials of BI-GLP1RA FRCs in adults with T2D were identified across major databases through 20 December 2025. Co-primary outcomes were changes in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and body weight. A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis, with BI as the reference, was conducted in R using netmeta. Certainty was assessed using Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA). Thirty trials involving 17,862 participants were included. All FRCs reduced HbA1c and body weight more than BI alone. For HbA1c, HR17031 had the largest estimated reduction (mean difference [MD]: -0.72%), followed by IDegLira (-0.64%) and iGlarLixi (-0.53%). For body weight, IcoSema had the largest estimated reduction (-3.16 kg), followed by HR17031 (-1.74 kg) and IDegLira (-1.65 kg). No HR17031 comparison with other FRCs was statistically significant for either co-primary outcome; its ranking is hypothesis-generating. Excluding the high-risk-of-bias trial produced broadly consistent estimates. Compared with BI, FRCs increased achievement of HbA1c < 7%, often without weight gain or clinically significant/severe hypoglycemia. CINeMA indicated predominantly low- to moderate-certainty evidence for FRC versus BI comparisons and low- to very low-certainty evidence for many indirect comparisons among active regimens. BI-GLP1RA FRCs improve glycemic control and weight outcomes compared with BI alone. Rankings and apparent differences among FRCs or versus other active regimens warrant cautious interpretation given heterogeneity, inconsistency, and limited certainty of indirect evidence.

title: Metabolic oncology: clonal selection and the pre-existing origins of cancer resistance.
abstract: Treatment resistance remains the principal cause of cancer mortality, conventionally modeled as an adaptive response arising under therapeutic pressure. However, a substantial component of resistance is plausibly established before therapeutic exposure, determined by the metabolic environment of the tissue in which the malignancy arises. This article advances the hypothesis that chronic metabolic dysregulation constitutes a selective pressure acting on premalignant tissue. Hyperinsulinemia and increased bioavailable IGF-1 sustain PI3K-AKT-mTOR and RAS-MAPK signaling in tissues where insulin resistance has preserved mitogenic sensitivity, creating an environment permissive to clonal selection. Metabolic intermediates serve as obligate substrates for chromatin-modifying enzymes, coupling metabolic state to the epigenome across the years of subclinical dysregulation that precede diagnosis. Within this landscape, hypoxia stabilizes G9a and promotes locus-specific H3K9 methylation at apoptotic and differentiation loci, whereas one-carbon and S-adenosylmethionine status determine the available H3K9me1 substrate pool. The consequence is an elevated apoptotic threshold and enrichment of epigenetically primed, apoptosis-resistant cells before a tumor is histologically apparent or clinically detected. The argument is fundamentally Darwinian: the metabolic environment selects its survivors before any therapeutic intervention. Clonal dynamics subsequently attributed to therapy may therefore reflect, in part, selection of a pre-existing, resistance-primed population. This is advanced not as an alternative to clonal evolution, of which selection of pre-existing clones is a constituent process, but as a determinant of the pre-treatment resistance heterogeneity upon which therapeutic pressure acts. Existing data on metabolic intervention are discordant, and the discrepancies appear more consistent with differences in intervention potency, timing, and trial design than with failure of the proposed mechanism. Much of the supporting evidence remains indirect and derives from heterogeneous experimental settings. The observations that would distinguish this framework from reverse causation and treatment-induced plasticity are specified, together with its central untested prediction: that pretreatment metabolic state correlates with baseline subclonal architecture, chromatin state, and treatment outcome.

title: Metabolic, hormonal, and reproductive effects of GLP-1 receptor agonizts in hyperandrogenic insulin-resistant women: a systematic review.
journal: Gynecological endocrinology : the official journal of the International Society of Gynecological Endocrinology
abstract: Hyperandrogenic insulin-resistant states, most commonly polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and severe phenotypes such as HAIR-AN syndrome, are characterized by metabolic dysfunction, androgen excess, and reproductive disturbance. Insulin resistance is a central pathogenic driver and therapeutic target. To systematically evaluate the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonizts on metabolic, hormonal, and reproductive outcomes in adult women with hyperandrogenic insulin-resistant states. Data Sources and Study Selection: A systematic search identified randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and case series evaluating GLP-1 receptor agonizts in PCOS and HAIR-AN syndrome, reflecting the heterogeneity of the current evidence base.Data extraction and synthesis Outcomes were synthesized across metabolic (anthropometric and glycaemic), hormonal, reproductive, dermatologic, and safety domains, accounting for heterogeneity in interventions and study designs. Metabolic responses appeared more consistent and robust than endocrine outcomes. Reproductive outcomes such as menstrual regularity were variably reported and showed inconsistent improvement across studies, limiting firm conclusions regarding fertility-related benefit. Evidence in severe phenotypes remains limited but suggestive of clinical benefit. GLP-1 receptor agonizts are a promising adjunctive therapy in hyperandrogenic insulin-resistant states, with the strongest evidence for metabolic improvement. Reproductive and endocrine outcomes remain less consistent, likely reflecting heterogeneity in study design, populations, and outcome reporting. Further high-quality, phenotype-specific trials are required.

title: Gastric residual volume in patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A comparative gastric ultrasound pilot study.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release, promote satiety, and may slow gastric emptying. Introduced in 2005 for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, these agents have prompted interest in assessing delayed gastric emptying as a potential biomarker to predict treatment response and to guide decisions regarding long-term therapy. Point-of-care gastric ultrasound (POCUS) offers a bedside method to assess gastric contents. To compare gastric residual volume (GRV) on gastric ultrasound among patients with obesity receiving GLP-1 RAs and nonusers and those with prior weight loss surgeries. In this comparative cross-sectional pilot study, gastric POCUS was done on patients with obesity who took GLP-1 RAs and other patients with obesity with no history of taking GLP-1 RAs prior to surgery in the supine and lateral decubitus positions. Antral cross-sectional area and GRV were measured using validated mathematical models. Patients receiving GLP-1 RAs demonstrated higher estimated GRV compared with nonusers. A higher proportion of GLP-1 RA users met ultrasound criteria for a full stomach. Among patients with obesity, GLP-1 RA therapy was associated with enlargement of the gastric antrum, increased gastric volume, and greater residual gastric contents, leading to an elevated estimated risk of aspiration. This increased risk is primarily determined by gastric ultrasound findings rather than patient characteristics, comorbidities, or duration of treatment. Gastric ultrasound may support individualized perioperative decision-making regarding aspiration precautions.

title: Digital Food Purchase Signatures and Their Response to GLP-1-Based Treatment in People With Obesity.
abstract: To characterise digital food purchase signatures in adults with obesity (OB) versus normal-weight (NW) controls and explore changes from pre-treatment to early (5-month) and later (10-month) phases of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) therapy, including high and low weight-loss responders. We obtained household-level loyalty-card food purchase data at two major Swiss grocery retailers for 56 OB adults and 92 NW controls, covering 12-24 months. Purchases were matched to a nutritional database and analysed by purchase patterns using nutrient profiles, food group distributions, and composite diet quality scores, comparing OB and NW cross-sectionally and, within the OB group, longitudinally following GLP-1RA initiation. Compared to NW (BMI 22.0 ± 1.7 kg/m2), OB participants (BMI 37.8 ± 5.2 kg/m2) purchased a higher proportion of energy from protein (mainly animal-based), higher energy-adjusted salt content, but smaller energy shares of fruit, vegetables, nuts, whole foods and scored lower on the Dietary Phytochemical Index, Simplified Healthy Food Diversity Index and alternate Mediterranean Diet Score (all p < 0.05). GLP-1RA initiation was followed by early increases in protein-derived energy, fibre content, energy from fruit, vegetables and unprocessed foods (all p < 0.05). However, by 10 months, purchasing patterns no longer differed meaningfully from pre-treatment levels in the full cohort. High/low weight-loss responders did not differ in food purchase patterns, except for a greater increase in salt content among low responders at 5 months. Distinct digital food purchase signatures were observed in OB versus NW adults. Within OB, no clear longitudinal shift was evident after 10 months of GLP-1RA treatment, although the sample size and household-level data limited individual-level precision and interpretability.

title: Semaglutide versus other GLP-1 RAs and cardiovascular risk in obesity-related cancer survivors.
abstract: Obesity-related cancer (ORCa) survivors are a unique population often excluded from landmark GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) trials. Given their cardiovascular risks, we investigated whether semaglutide initiation, compared with other GLP-1 RA, was associated with modified 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) among ORCa survivors with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We emulated a target trial using PCORnet-UTSW electronic health records (2016-2025). Adults with ORCa and T2D initiating semaglutide versus other GLP-1 RA were included. The primary outcome was modified 3-point MACE (myocardial infarction, stroke, or all-cause mortality). Cumulative incidence risk (CIR), risk difference (RD), and hazard ratio (HR) were estimated in 1:1 propensity score-matched cohort. Among 918 matched patients (semaglutide, n = 459; other GLP-1 RA, n = 459), 124 modified 3-point MACE occurred. The 5-year CIR% was 17.6 (95% CI, 12.3-22.9) for semaglutide and 26.6 (95% CI, 20.7-32.6) for other GLP-1 RA. Semaglutide was associated with lower modified 3-point MACE risk (RD%, -7.41 [95% CI, -11.83 to - 2.98];HR, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.44-0.94]) than other GLP-1 RA. Findings were largely consistent across high-risk subgroups. Semaglutide was associated with a lower modified 3-point MACE risk than other GLP-1 RA. These findings suggest potential heterogeneity in cardioprotective effects and warrant confirmation.

title: Insights from multi-omics on GLP-1 receptor agonists in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
abstract: Glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the management of T2D and obesity. T2D clustering highlights distinct phenotypes that differ in GLP-1RA benefit. While they have markedly improved quality of life for many individuals, converging evidence indicates that genetic variation, metabolomic remodeling, and gut microbiota composition contribute to substantial inter-individual variability in GLP-1RA efficacy and tolerability. GLP-1RAs, in return, can variably affect the metabolome and microbiome composition in treated individuals. This review focuses on human multi-omics GLP-1RA intervention studies, complemented by relevant mechanistic preclinical evidence. Genetic variation in GLP1R, TCF7L2, and other loci has been associated with differences in glycaemic and weight outcomes, although most findings remain preliminary, inconsistent across populations, or not yet replicated. Pharmacometabolomic studies show recurrent of lipid-related pathways including, glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, ceramides, amino acids, and bile acids, with drug-specific signatures. GLP-1RAs are also associated with changes in gut microbial composition, including taxa such as Akkermansia and Bacteroides, although the direction and clinical significance of these changes vary across studies due to methodological and population heterogeneity. Multi-omics and AI-based models show promise for predicting treatment response by integrating genetic, metabolic, microbial, and clinical data to supporting more effective and individualized therapy and advancing precision medicine.

title: Cardiovascular Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Across Age Groups: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
abstract: To evaluate whether cardiovascular effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) differ by age. PubMed and Embase were searched to 1 July 2026 for randomized placebo-controlled GLP-1RA trials in adults with type 2 diabetes or overweight/obesity reporting age-stratified major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke). Hazard ratios (HRs) for participants aged < 65 and ≥ 65 years were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Effect modification was assessed by pooling trial-specific ratios of HRs (RHRs) for ≥ 65 versus < 65 years. Where reported, effects were assessed across < 65, 65 to < 75 and ≥ 75 years. Eight trials (SUSTAIN-6, EXSCEL, Harmony Outcomes, PIONEER 6, REWIND, AMPLITUDE-O, SELECT and SOUL) comprising 71 926 participants were included. GLP-1RAs reduced MACE at < 65 years and ≥ 65 years, with pooled HRs of 0.81 (95% CI 0.69-0.94; I2 = 64.1%) and 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.90; I2 = 0.0%), respectively. The pooled RHR showed no clear evidence of effect modification (1.03, 95% CI 0.85-1.25), although between-trial heterogeneity was high (I2 = 59.3%). Among trials reporting three age strata, RHRs showed no clear evidence of effect modification for 65 to < 75 or ≥ 75 years versus < 65 years, but data were available from only four trials, and the ≥ 75-year group was relatively small. Across the included trial populations, GLP-1RAs lowered MACE in the age groups examined, with no clear evidence that relative cardiovascular effects differed by age.

title: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies for Child and Adolescent Obesity: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Childhood obesity is a chronic, multifactorial disease requiring attention to biological, behavioral, psychological, family, and socioeconomic factors. This narrative review examined the integration of lifestyle, family-based, psychological, and pharmacological approaches, focusing on treatment engagement, eating disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and treatment durability. A single search interface covering PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science (the University of Turin library discovery platform) was used to identify studies published primarily from 2010 to August 2026. Pediatric trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and public-health reports were prioritized. Intensive family-based, multicomponent behavioral treatment remains the best-supported foundation of care, although psychological outcomes are infrequently assessed. Psychiatric comorbidity is heterogeneous; loss-of-control eating, emotional symptoms, ADHD, and executive-function difficulties may impair engagement in selected patients, and untreated ADHD has been associated with a slower BMI response to weight management. Professionally supervised obesity treatment containing a dietary component did not, on average, worsen eating psychopathology and reduced several related symptoms. Family participation improved outcomes, whereas logistical, socioeconomic, and psychological barriers reduced attendance. Across randomized trials, adding anti-obesity medication to behavioral treatment produced an additional, although on average modest, reduction in BMI. Semaglutide, liraglutide, and phentermine/topiramate produced larger numerical reductions than older agents in separate trials, but heterogeneity and the absence of head-to-head comparisons preclude formal ranking. Gastrointestinal adverse events were frequent with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Pediatric trials and real-world evidence indicate partial weight regain after discontinuation, while prescribing remains limited and unequal. Pediatric obesity care should be phenotype-informed, multidisciplinary, and longitudinal. Pharmacotherapy can enhance BMI reduction but should complement rather than replace behavioral, psychological, and family care. Outcomes should extend beyond BMI to metabolic, psychological, functional, and long-term measures.

title: A retrospective real-world study on semaglutide effectiveness in patients with obesity: differences between patients with and without food craving.
abstract: Food craving (FC) is an established predictor of obesity. However, its role in weight management is insufficiently addressed in routine clinical practice. This retrospective study included adults with obesity, stratified by FC status, to compare the effectiveness of semaglutide plus hypocaloric diet (semaglutide group) versus hypocaloric diet alone (control group) in reducing body weight (BW). Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), 3 months (T3), and 6 months (T6). The primary outcome was the between-group comparison of changes in BW from baseline at T3 and T6, also stratified by FC status. Secondary outcomes included changes in body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC). 120 patients with obesity (mean age ± SD: 51.0 ± 15.9 years; 70% female) were included. Of these, 67 (56%) received semaglutide plus hypocaloric diet and 53 (44%) diet alone. FC was present in 53% of patients and was more frequent in women and younger individuals. BW, BMI, and WC significantly decreased in both semaglutide and control group over time (all p <0.0001). However, at 6 months, semaglutide group achieved greater reductions in BW (-3.3 kg; p=0.0004), BMI (-1.8 kg/m2; p=0.0015), and WC (-2.3 cm; p=0.03) compared with controls. Differences in BW reduction were maintained across patients with FC (-3.1 kg, p=0.03) and without FC (-3.4 kg; p=0.007). Semaglutide plus hypocaloric diet treatment is more effective than hypocaloric diet alone for weight reduction in real-world clinical practice, even in the presence of FC. Assessing FC may support more individualized obesity management strategies.

title: Cardiometabolic Substrate Modification in Atrial Fibrillation: Obesity and Epicardial Adipose Tissue in the Era of Incretin-Based Therapies and Catheter Ablation.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is increasingly understood as the electrical expression of a systemic and atrial cardiometabolic disease rather than an isolated disorder of pulmonary-vein triggers. Obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, sleep-disordered breathing, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and visceral adiposity promote atrial stretch, inflammation, fibrosis, autonomic imbalance, and conduction heterogeneity. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), particularly the peri-left-atrial depot, may provide a local mechanistic bridge between systemic metabolic dysfunction and atrial cardiomyopathy through paracrine, inflammatory, fibrotic, and infiltrative pathways. This framework has direct therapeutic implications. Structured weight loss, cardiorespiratory fitness, alcohol reduction, and comprehensive risk-factor management can reduce AF burden and improve rhythm-control outcomes, although the magnitude of benefit varies across populations and trial designs. Incretin-based therapies have introduced a potentially important pharmacologic route to substrate modification. Semaglutide and tirzepatide produce substantial weight loss and favorable cardiovascular and heart-failure effects, while emerging observational and prospective data suggest lower AF incidence and post-ablation recurrence. However, evidence for reduced post-ablation recurrence remains predominantly non-randomized and is susceptible to residual confounding, treatment-selection effects, and healthy-user bias. Causality, weight-independent antiarrhythmic effects, optimal timing relative to ablation, and durability after treatment withdrawal remain unresolved. Observational sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor data support further investigation of cardiometabolic approaches to rhythm control, although randomized evidence has not consistently demonstrated benefit. Our review integrates mechanistic, imaging, lifestyle, pharmacologic, and electrophysiological evidence and proposes a practical model in which catheter ablation and cardiometabolic substrate modification are complementary strategies.

title: Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders treated with antipsychotics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
abstract: Weight gain and impaired glucose metabolism are common complications of antipsychotic treatment in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD). While beneficial in other populations, the efficacy and safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) in SSD remain unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating GLP-1 RAs versus placebo in SSD patients treated with antipsychotics. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched until January 2026. Random-effects models were used to pool mean differences (MDs), standardized mean differences (SMDs), and risk ratios (RRs), as appropriate. Seven RCTs including 481 participants were included. Compared with placebo, GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD -6.98 kg; 95% CI -10.53 to -3.43), BMI (MD -2.51 kg/m²; 95% CI -3.51 to -1.51), waist circumference (MD -5.05 cm; 95% CI -6.66 to -3.44), HbA1c (MD -0.32 percentage points; 95% CI -0.38 to -0.26), and fasting blood glucose (MD -0.54 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.83 to -0.25). Heterogeneity was substantial for body weight (I²=93%) and BMI (I²=80%). No significant effects emerged for blood pressure or lipid parameters. Psychiatric symptom severity did not differ between GLP-1 RAs and placebo (SMD -0.05; 95% CI -0.36 to 0.25). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with GLP-1 RAs than with placebo, while overall study drop-out did not differ between groups. GLP-1 RAs improve short-term anthropometric and glycemic outcomes in SSD patients treated with antipsychotics. However, the limited number of trials, substantial heterogeneity in weight-related outcomes, and relatively short follow-up warrant cautious interpretation and further large-scale RCTs.

title: Parasympathetic dysfunction assessed by deep-breathing CVR-R is associated with early discontinuation of oral semaglutide in type 2 diabetes: A multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Although glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists are widely used for type 2 diabetes, gastrointestinal intolerance frequently leads to early discontinuation. Predictors of oral semaglutide discontinuation remain poorly defined, and its formulation-specific dependence on gastric conditions may influence tolerability. We examined whether the coefficient of variation of R-R intervals (CVR-R) was associated with discontinuation within 6 months. In this multicenter retrospective study, 203 consecutive patients initiating oral semaglutide between February 2021 and December 2024 were screened, and 61 were analyzed after exclusions. The Discontinuation Group (n = 21) discontinued because of nausea and/or vomiting within 6 months, whereas the Maintenance Group (n = 40) continued for ≥ 6 months. CVR-R was assessed at rest (CVR-R_rest) and during deep breathing (CVR-R_DB). Associations with discontinuation were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression; exploratory machine learning and time-to-event analyses were performed. CVR-R_DB was lower in the Discontinuation Group than in the Maintenance Group (median 1.93% vs 3.26%, P < 0.001). CVR-R_DB remained independently associated with discontinuation after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted OR 0.191; 95% CI 0.071-0.512; P = 0.001; AUC 0.832) and further adjustment for neuropathy stage. The AUC was numerically higher for the age- and sex-adjusted model containing CVR-R_DB than for that containing CVR-R_rest (0.832 vs 0.699; DeLong P = 0.085). An internally derived CVR-R_DB cutoff of 2.55% stratified 6-month persistence (43.3% vs 87.1%; log-rank P < 0.001), and machine learning analyses prioritized CVR-R_DB. Lower CVR-R during deep breathing was associated with early oral semaglutide discontinuation due to nausea and/or vomiting. CVR-R_DB may support risk stratification at initiation.

title: Effects of liraglutide on blood pressure and renal function in patients with type 2 diabetic nephropathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract: The effects of liraglutide on blood pressure in patients with T2DN remain unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of liraglutide on blood pressure and renal function in patients with T2DN. We conducted comprehensive searches of Web of Science, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Elsevier ScienceDirect, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and VIP databases. Eligible studies were RCTs of ≥12 weeks' duration evaluating liraglutide for T2DN. Two independent reviewers screened citations, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Tool. Statistical analyses were performed in Stata 17.0 and RevMan 5.4, with effect sizes presented as RR or MD and 95% CI. The Cochrane Q test and I2 statistic were used to quantify statistical heterogeneity. This meta-analysis included 23 RCTs involving 1,723 participants. Compared with the control group, liraglutide significantly reduced SBP [MD = -5.00, 95% CI (-7.17, -2.84)], while no significant effect was observed on DBP. In addition, liraglutide was associated with favorable changes in some renal biomarkers, as evidenced by reductions in Scr, UACR, Cys-C, BUN, and β2-MG, as well as elevations in eGFR. Improvements were also observed in glycemic control, lipid profiles, BMI, and inflammatory markers. Subgroup analyses indicated dose-dependent differences in UACR and LDL-C. In addition, both UACR and Scr were affected by intervention-regimen type, while HbA1c was affected by baseline albuminuria category. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, and adjustment for publication bias did not alter the statistical significance of the key outcomes. Liraglutide may be associated with favorable changes in selected BP, renal, metabolic, and inflammatory outcomes in patients with T2DN. However, further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251232844, PROSPERO CRD420251232844.

title: Closing the Gap to Bariatric Surgery: Predictors of Non-Progression in Patients with Obesity Class IV and V at a Community-Based Bariatric Center.
journal: Journal of laparoendoscopic & advanced surgical techniques. Part A
abstract: Patients with obesity class IV and V benefit substantially from bariatric surgery, yet many do not complete the preoperative pathway. The contribution of system-level barriers and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) therapy to non-progression remains poorly understood, particularly in community settings. We conducted a single-center retrospective study of adults with obesity class IV and V evaluated for bariatric surgery (2024-2025). The primary outcome was progression to surgery. Variables included demographics, comorbidities, insurance, primary care physician (PCP) status, GLP-1 RA use, specialist consultation completion, prior authorization activity, and surgeon follow-up. Chi-square testing, stratified odds ratios, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Among 73 patients, 38 (52.1%) did not progress to surgery. Demographics and comorbidities were similar between groups. Patients who did not progress had lower PCP establishment (44.7% versus 97.1%, P < .001), fewer completed specialist consultations (28.9% versus 71.4%, P = .001), fewer nutrition visits (P = .004), and fewer surgeon follow-up visits (P < .001). GLP-1 RA use at initial consultation was associated with lower progression to surgery (57.9% versus 11.4%, OR 0.12, P = .008), with consistent findings across insurance types but a weaker association among patients without an established PCP. Patients who did not progress also had higher emergency department utilization and more system-related scheduling barriers (both P < .001). Non-progression to bariatric surgery was associated with modifiable system-level barriers, including limited PCP integration, incomplete specialist evaluation, and reduced surgical follow-up. GLP-1 RA use at presentation was also associated with non-progression, although this relationship may reflect differences in treatment pathways rather than a direct treatment effect. Structured patient navigation and integrated medical-surgical obesity care may improve pathway completion.

title: Beyond LDL-C: A case-based review of complex Dyslipidemia.
journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
abstract: Dyslipidemia is clinically heterogeneous, and LDL-C alone may not fully capture atherogenic particle burden, metabolic risk, treatment response, or inherited disease. This case-based review presents three dyslipidemia phenotypes that illustrate common diagnostic and management challenges. The first case describes diet-sensitive LDL particle and lipoprotein insulin resistance changes despite LDL-C values near conventional targets in a patient with subclinical coronary atherosclerosis. The second highlights persistent low HDL-C and HDL particle number despite substantial LDL-C reduction with non-statin and incretin-era therapies in the setting of obesity and strong family history. The third demonstrates genetically confirmed familial hypercholesterolemia due to a pathogenic LDLR variant despite absent classic physical stigmata. Together, these cases support a phenotype-driven approach that integrates LDL-C, ApoB or LDL particle number, diet response, metabolic context, imaging, medication tolerance, and selective genetic testing to individualize dyslipidemia risk assessment and treatment.

title: Association of GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use with Thyroid Outcomes in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus, but their associations with thyroid disorders remain uncertain. We evaluated whether initiating a GLP-1 RA, compared with initiating a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i), was associated with newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis and other thyroid outcomes. This new-user, active-comparator cohort study emulated a target trial using the TriNetX Collaborative Network. Adults with type 2 diabetes who initiated a GLP-1 RA or DPP-4i between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022, and had no prior use of either drug class were eligible. Patients with pre-existing thyroid disease, any neoplasm, immunosuppressant or immunostimulant use, transplantation, or end-stage kidney disease or dialysis were excluded. Propensity score matching yielded 107,912 patients per group. The primary outcome was newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis; secondary outcomes were nontoxic uninodular goiter, nontoxic multinodular goiter, and thyroid malignancy. Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with false discovery rate adjustment. Follow-up extended from 1 day after treatment initiation to 4 years. Autoimmune thyroiditis occurred in 524 GLP-1 RA users (0.49%) and 417 DPP-4i users (0.39%). GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with a higher risk of autoimmune thyroiditis (HR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11-1.43; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002). Modestly higher risks were also observed for nontoxic uninodular goiter (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.13) and nontoxic multinodular goiter (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.03-1.19). The risk of thyroid malignancy did not differ significantly (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.77-1.12). Findings were generally consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses, although heterogeneity was observed across body mass index strata. Among adults with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with small increases in newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis and benign nodular thyroid disease, but not with thyroid malignancy. Given the small absolute differences and the potential for residual confounding and surveillance bias, these findings require validation in future studies.

title: Dissecting polycystic metabolic ovarian syndrome heterogeneity (PMOS): multi-omics, AI subtyping, and precision management.
abstract: Polycystic metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) is the most common endocrine disorder, affecting 8-12% of women of reproductive age and increasing the risk of infertility, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease. However, traditional symptom-based diagnostic criteria do not fully capture the underlying biological diversity of PMOS. Recent research using multi-omics and artificial intelligence (AI) has revealed that PMOS is best understood as a syndrome with multiple subtypes. Data-driven clustering of clinical variables consistently identifies four major subtypes: HA-PCOS, OB-PCOS, SHBG-PCOS, and LH-PCOS. Each subtype shows unique hormonal, metabolic, and genetic features, including distinct patterns in lipid, amino acid, and energy metabolism. Immune system disruptions and impaired blood clot breakdown in the ovarian environment are also notable features. Novel findings suggest that altered lactate metabolism and changes in histone lactylation may contribute to granulosa cell dysfunction, although further studies are needed to confirm these mechanisms. Machine learning models that integrate clinical, metabolic, and genetic data have achieved high diagnostic accuracy and can provide interpretable results. Potential targeted therapies, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, N-acetylcysteine, and NK3R antagonists, have been proposed for specific subtypes, but have yet to be validated in clinical trials. Remaining challenges include small and homogeneous study cohorts, limited long-term data, and barriers to care in low-resource settings. Overall, recognizing PMOS as a syndrome with distinct subtypes highlights the promise of AI-powered, personalized approaches for more effective and equitable management.

title: 12-month weight-loss trajectories and predictors of response to tirzepatide under individualized dosing: A multicenter real-world study.
abstract: Real-world evidence on 12-month treatment effectiveness and persistence with tirzepatide remains limited, particularly under individualized dosing and self-funded treatment conditions. We evaluated 12-month tirzepatide outcomes in routine clinical practice. This was a multicenter, retrospective, observational real-world study including 249 adults with overweight or obesity treated with tirzepatide across 13 obesity practices in Greece. Treatment was entirely self-funded, and dose escalation was individualized rather than protocol driven. Treatment persistence, reasons for discontinuation, weight loss, dose trajectories, metabolic outcomes, and predictors of 12-month response were evaluated. At 12 months, 170/249 patients (68.3%) remained on treatment, 64 (25.7%) had confirmed discontinuation, and 15 (6.0%) were lost to follow-up. Among patients with available weight measurements, mean weight loss was 19.9 ± 8.6% at 12 months, with 88.9%, 50.0%, and 27.2% achieving ≥10%, ≥20%, and ≥25% weight loss, respectively. Mean tirzepatide dose at 12 months was 9.71 mg. Among 179 patients assessed at both 6 and 12 months, 70.4% experienced >2% additional weight loss during the second 6 months, whereas 10.1% experienced >2% weight regain. Six-month percentage weight loss was not significantly associated with additional weight loss between months 6 and 12 after multivariable adjustment (β = -0.110, P = 0.135). Among 139 participants who had not achieved ≥20% weight loss at month 6, early response demonstrated moderate discrimination for achieving this cumulative threshold at month 12 (AUC 0.760, 95% bootstrap CI 0.675-0.837), with an adjusted OR of 1.34 per additional percentage point of 6-month weight loss (P < 0.001). In a fully self-funded real-world setting, tirzepatide was associated with substantial weight loss and high documented treatment persistence over 12 months. Six-month weight-loss response was associated with the likelihood of achieving ≥20% weight loss at 12 months. These findings do not establish long-term weight maintenance beyond the observation period.

title: Decoding the Safety Profile of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Facts, Myths, and Ongoing Controversies.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) represent one of the most significant therapeutic advances in the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. As their indications have expanded to include cardiovascular and kidney disease, safety concerns involving multiple organ systems have received increasing attention. This narrative review examines the spectrum of adverse effects linked to GLP-1RAs and provides a clinically relevant platform for assessing their safe prescription. Gastrointestinal intolerance, modest increases in heart rate, and a modest but reproducible increase in the risk of gallbladder and biliary disease represent the most consistently supported adverse effects of GLP-1RAs. A risk of pancreatitis is also considered to exist, although some studies have challenged this association. Conversely, correlations with neuropsychiatric and dermatological disorders, diabetic retinopathy, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, perioperative aspiration, sexual and reproductive disturbances, sarcopenia, and malignancy remain controversial. Most available evidence derives from pharmacovigilance databases, retrospective observational studies, and secondary analyses of randomized trials, which are limited by reporting bias, residual confounding, and inability to establish causality.
